issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court should not disturb concurrent findings on witness evidence in a special-leave criminal appeal without an extraordinary showing of gross and palpable injustice.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both accepted the eyewitness evidence, which was corroborated by the dying declaration and medical evidence.

The appellants repeated challenges to the witnesses’ relationships, the medical evidence, and the injuries to the accused, but the Court found no serious infirmity in the evidence or extraordinary injustice.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the concurrent findings of the courts below.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court is very slow to interfere with concurrent conclusions on appreciation of witness evidence; an appellant must make out an extraordinary case of gross and palpable injustice. The Court applied this principle to the findings affirmed by the High Court.

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_evidence_findings: The trial court and appellate court reached the same findings on the evidence.
predicates.no_extraordinary_gross_injustice_shown: The appellant did not establish an extraordinary case of gross and palpable injustice.

issues.definition: When a special-leave criminal appeal challenges concurrent evidence findings and no extraordinary gross injustice is shown, the Supreme Court does not interfere with those findings.

issues.legal_issue: Members of an unlawful assembly may be liable for murder when a member commits the killing in pursuit of the assembly’s object or the members knew such an offence was likely in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: The accused approached the deceased together while armed with a spear, a gandasa, and lathis.

One accused restrained the deceased and urged the others to attack; another rejected the proposal to settle the dispute elsewhere, and the group then carried out a coordinated attack that caused fatal injuries.
The Court found that the accused acted together and knew the fatal consequence of their attack, even if the assembly’s original object had been only to beat the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The accused were guilty of murder read with the unlawful-assembly liability rule; the Court found no basis to reduce the offence to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes liability where an offence is committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly’s common object or is one the members knew to be likely in prosecution of that object. The Court relied on K.C. Mathew and Others v. State of Travancore-Cochin, [1955] 3 S.C.R. 1057, and explained that an assembly’s original object of beating may encompass a connected fatal attack when the members knew the weapons’ use was likely to cause death. It distinguished the authorities cited by the appellants, Shambhu Nath Singh v. State of Bihar, AIR 1960 SC 725, and The Queen v. Sabid Ali, 1873 Weekly Reporter (20), 5.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_murder_case and members_joined_coordinated_attack and deadly_weapons_used and members_knew_death_was_likely_in_pursuit_of_object

predicates.unlawful_assembly_murder_case: The proceeding concerns murder liability attributed to members of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.members_joined_coordinated_attack: The accused acted together in a coordinated attack on the victim.
predicates.deadly_weapons_used: Members of the assembly used weapons capable of causing death.
predicates.members_knew_death_was_likely_in_pursuit: The members knew that using the weapons in pursuit of the assembly’s object was likely to cause death.

issues.definition: When members of an unlawful assembly join a coordinated attack using deadly weapons and know death is likely in pursuit of the assembly’s object, they are liable for murder through the assembly.

issues.legal_issue: Use of wording that describes an assault as a beating in the charge does not invalidate the conviction when the accused were not prejudiced by that wording.
material_facts: The charge used the word “beat” in describing the attack.

The evidence accepted by the courts established the accused’s participation in the fatal attack, and the manner in which the defence was conducted showed that the accused were not prejudiced by the wording.
issues.conclusion: The Court found that the wording of the charge did not prejudice the accused and did not disturb the conviction on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the wording of the charge in light of the evidence and the conduct of the defence at trial, and found no prejudice from the use of the word “beat.”

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial resulting in a conviction.
predicates.charge_used_less_severe_attack_descripti: The charge described the alleged attack in terms less severe than the fatal offence ultimately established.
predicates.defence_conduct_shows_no_prejudice_from_: The way the defence responded to the prosecution case shows that the wording did not prejudice the accused.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, a less severe description of the attack in the charge does not invalidate the conviction when the defence was not prejudiced by that wording.

issues.legal_issue: Separate convictions for unlawful-assembly offences are unnecessary in the circumstances once the convictions for murder through unlawful-assembly liability are affirmed.
material_facts: The Court affirmed the convictions for murder read with the unlawful-assembly liability rule.
Some of the accused also had separate convictions under the unlawful-assembly offence provision; the Court expressly set aside the convictions and sentences under that provision for three accused.
issues.conclusion: The Court stated that no further separate conviction under the unlawful-assembly offence provisions was necessary in the circumstances, set aside the specified convictions and sentences under the rioting provision, and otherwise affirmed the convictions for murder through unlawful-assembly liability.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, in the circumstances of this case, separate convictions under Sections 147 and 148 of the Indian Penal Code were not further necessary once all the accused were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 149; the operative order expressly set aside the convictions under Section 147 for three accused.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case involving unlawful-assembly liability.
predicates.murder_liability_through_unlawful_assemb: The court affirms murder liability attributed to the accused as members of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.separate_assembly_offence_conviction_is_: A separate conviction for an unlawful-assembly offence has also been recorded against an accused.

issues.definition: When murder liability through unlawful-assembly membership is affirmed and a separate unlawful-assembly offence conviction is also recorded, that separate conviction is unnecessary in these circumstances.
